Who painted Gloucester and Cape Ann, and when
Each bar runs from a painter’s earliest to latest dated work in this brief; undated works are left out. Darker bars mark the painters of the nine mapped sites.

Gloucester’s own Fitz Henry Lane painted his harbor from the 1840s until his death in 1865, with Mary Blood Mellen working beside him. Winslow Homer spent the summers of 1873 and 1880 here; his oils are at the National Gallery of Art and the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, and his watercolors at the Met, the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Philadelphia Museum of Art, Princeton and elsewhere.⟦0⟧ Childe Hassam’s harbor views of about 1899 are at the Norton Museum of Art and the Newark Museum, and his 1918–19 pictures at the Met, PAFA and the Harn.

Hunt and Bricher came in the 1870s; Twachtman, Metcalf, Duveneck, Beaux and Prendergast around the turn of the century; then Hopper, Sloan, Davis, Demuth and Hartley, Milton Avery and the young Mark Rothko and Adolph Gottlieb, and the Rocky Neck and Rockport colonies. This brief catalogues 131 of their Gloucester and Cape Ann works, by 35 painters, nearly all in 48 public collections. A November 2026 update adds sixteen more, by Mary Blood Mellen, Charles Demuth, Mark Rothko, Theresa Bernstein, Nell Blaine, Max Kuehne and Earl Horter.

Born in Gloucester in 1804, Lane painted its harbor, Ten Pound Island, Stage Fort, Eastern Point and Norman's Woe for two decades. The Cape Ann Museum holds the largest group of his pictures; it has no stable object pages, so its holdings are cited through its own catalogue raisonné, ⟦0⟧Fitz Henry Lane Online⟦1⟧.⟦2⟧ The NGA's 2025.89 numbers mark a recent gift, and its links may change. Before painting full time he worked in lithography shops; the Cape Ann Museum also holds his first known work, a watercolor of 1830, about 100 drawings and all three of his lithographed views of Gloucester.⟦3⟧ From the mid-1850s Mary Blood Mellen worked beside him, free to copy his drawings and at times his canvases; one painting, ⟦4⟧Coast of Maine⟦5⟧, bears both their signatures.

Homer spent summer 1873 in Gloucester at the Atlantic House, and summer 1880 on Ten Pound Island with the lighthouse keeper, Oliver Merrill. He did not work there again (⟦0⟧MFA Boston, “When Homer Went to Gloucester”⟦1⟧).⟦2⟧ The NGA's Gallery M68 hangs ⟦3⟧“Dad's Coming!”⟦4⟧ and ⟦5⟧Breezing Up⟦6⟧ side by side. His 1880 ⟦7⟧Eastern Point Light⟦8⟧ is Gloucester's lighthouse; his better-known ⟦9⟧Eastern Point⟦10⟧ of 1900 is Prouts Neck, Maine. In Gloucester he left the studio to work outdoors, and there he made himself a master of watercolor, almost to the exclusion of oil.

Hunt spent summer 1877 at Magnolia, at Gloucester's western edge. He painted his ⟦0⟧Gloucester Harbor⟦1⟧ outdoors in a single afternoon at Kettle Cove, which the MFA calls “a fishing village in Gloucester”; Kettle Cove sits on the Magnolia–Manchester line.⟦2⟧⟦3⟧ Bricher worked the beaches of Cape Ann in the mid-1870s. Hunt had brought the ideas of the French Barbizon painters to Boston, taught John La Farge and William and Henry James, and from 1868 opened his classes to women. His Magnolia studio drew other painters to Cape Ann, and it was probably through him that Frank Duveneck first heard of it.

Hassam's harbor views date from about 1899; the church, street and hilltop pictures, and his ⟦0⟧Inner Harbor, Gloucester⟦1⟧ prints, from 1918–19 and after. The Norton's ⟦2⟧Gloucester Harbor⟦3⟧ is the picture most often reproduced.

Twachtman spent his last three summers in Gloucester, painting the harbor from East Gloucester. His catalogue raisonné dates ⟦0⟧Fishing Boats at Gloucester⟦1⟧ to about 1900 (OP.1420) and lists Gloucester oils in at least six museums.⟦2⟧ That last summer he lived in a small cottage studio over the water at the Harbor View Hotel; Duveneck was painting beside him only days before his sudden death in August 1902.⟦3⟧⟦4⟧ His pupil Leon Kroll would bring Edward Hopper to Gloucester in 1912.

Prendergast painted Gloucester from about 1907 into the early 1920s: the harbor from the hills of East Gloucester, Bass Rocks and the beaches and bathhouses of Annisquam. The largest group is at the Williams College Museum of Art, from the artist's family. He sketched lightly in pencil and then let the watercolor wander from it, turning figures into rocks and sharpening edges with touches of pastel.

Painters of the 1880s to 1910s who left Gloucester and Cape Ann pictures in public collections: Willard Metcalf and Frank Duveneck, who summered in East Gloucester; Cecilia Beaux, who built her house and studio there; H. Bolton Jones and Sarah Wyman Whitman. Sanford Gifford’s sketches of 1864–65 at Manchester-by-the-Sea, on Cape Ann’s southwest shore, are included too. Duveneck brought a summer class from Boston and Cincinnati in 1890, apparently the first large class of its kind in town, and came back for about fifteen summers; he is said to have kept two studios, one for the morning light and one for the afternoon.⟦0⟧⟦1⟧ Beaux, the first woman to teach at the Pennsylvania Academy, first came with her family in the mid-1880s and by 1906 had built Green Alley on Eastern Point.

Hopper painted Gloucester in 1912 and again in 1923–28; Brooklyn bought six of his Gloucester watercolors in 1923.⟦0⟧ Sloan summered there in 1914–18; Davis returned from 1915 into the 1930s; Hartley painted Dogtown Common in 1931 and 1934; Avery summered in Gloucester most years from 1920 to 1945.⟦1⟧ To stay clear of copyright questions, these later works are listed with links to each museum's own image rather than reproduced. Hopper first came with his friend Leon Kroll, and in 1923 took up watercolor at the urging of Josephine Nivison, whom he married the next year.⟦2⟧ Sloan came on the advice of Charles Winter and in 1915 invited Stuart Davis, who called Gloucester the place he had been looking for.⟦3⟧⟦4⟧ Hartley kept away from the waterfront and walked into Dogtown, which he likened to Easter Island and Stonehenge.

From the 1910s Rocky Neck in East Gloucester, and Rockport across the cape, drew working colonies of painters. The Rockport Art Association holds many of their pictures but has no searchable online catalogue.⟦0⟧ These are the colony works confirmed in other public collections. Emile Gruppé opened the Gloucester School of Art on Rocky Neck in 1929 and ran it for thirty years.⟦1⟧ In 1922 the North Shore Arts Association, which juried its shows, and the Gloucester Society of Artists, which refused juries, were founded half a mile apart on Eastern Point Road.

Sixteen works added after further research. ⟦0⟧Mary Blood Mellen⟦1⟧, Lane’s student and collaborator in the 1850s, is now credited with pictures once given to Lane. ⟦2⟧Charles Demuth⟦3⟧ spent the summer of 1919 in Gloucester, breaking its wharves and houses into the faceted planes that became Precisionism. ⟦4⟧Mark Rothko⟦5⟧ and ⟦6⟧Adolph Gottlieb⟦7⟧ came at Milton Avery’s invitation in the early 1930s; in the summer of 1934 Rothko rented a house on Calder Street in East Gloucester and painted the fish wharfs of the Inner Harbor, the beach and his friends at handball. The Rothko catalogue raisonné lists 38 Gloucester works on paper, 24 of them in public collections; the Rothko trail on the website lists them all. The Cape Ann Museum’s 2026 exhibition ⟦8⟧Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea⟦9⟧ told that story and is at the Phillips Collection, Washington, from October 24, 2026, to January 24, 2027; in August 2026 Christopher Rothko gave the museum one of his father’s Gloucester watercolors. ⟦10⟧Theresa Bernstein⟦11⟧ painted Gloucester from 1916 until nearly the end of her 111 years, and ⟦12⟧Nell Blaine⟦13⟧ worked on Rocky Neck in the 1950s and summered in East Gloucester from 1974 to 1996. Max Kuehne’s and Earl Horter’s Gloucester oils come from the Whitney’s open collection data. The two Demuths and the Mellen are public domain and are reproduced here; the later works are in copyright and are listed with links to each museum’s own image.

Nine sites where a painting in this brief can be tied to a place on the ground. Each shows the painting beside a map: a dark circle where the painter stood, a diamond for the subject, the distance and direction between them, and where the sun would be at the hour the painting suggests, worked out for real dates in 2027.

Tags on each site say how firm the vantage point is. Map data: MassGIS (the dashed brown line is the historic high-water line, before the harbor was filled) and OpenStreetMap place points.⟦0⟧⟦1⟧ Stage Fort and Hunt's Kettle Cove picture are left out: their standing points are not documented closely enough to map.

Gloucester Harbor (NOAA station 8441841) has a mean range of 8.8 feet, and nearly 9.6 feet on the larger daily tides.⟦0⟧ Coves like Smith Cove and Wonson's Cove look completely different at high and low water, so check the tide table and plan each session around it.

From Memorial Day weekend to Labor Day, non-residents must reserve beach parking in advance through Blinkay, up to 10 days ahead. In 2026 Stage Fort Park cost $30 on weekdays and $35 on weekends and holidays.

The Rocky Neck Art Colony's Art Trail marks the historic painting sites of East Gloucester.⟦0⟧ Cape Ann Plein Air runs each autumn across Gloucester, Rockport, Essex, Manchester and Ipswich; the 2026 event was October 3–11.
Several historic vantage points, Banner Hill among them, are now private.⟦0⟧ Paint from roads, public ways and beaches, and ask before setting up on anyone's land.
Most of these pictures were painted in summer. The sun rises and sets well north of east and west in June, and moves south through the autumn. Compass directions are from true north.
Lane⟦0⟧ favored late-afternoon and sunset light, with the sun low in the west, and worked from measured drawings made on the spot.
Metcalf⟦0⟧ and the Banner Hill impressionists worked in the morning, with the sun behind them and the town lit full-face.
Homer⟦0⟧ in 1880 painted sunsets and moonlight from the middle of the harbor.
